title: Busiest Meeting Room
statement:
An office has n meeting rooms numbered 0 to n − 1. You get a list of meetings, where [start, end] books the half-open time range [start, end). All start times are different. The list is not sorted.

Meetings are handled in order of their start time:

  • A meeting goes to the lowest-numbered room that is free at its start time. A room whose meeting ends at time t is free at t.
  • If no room is free, the meeting waits for the room that frees up first (the lowest number if several free up at once). It keeps its original length, so it ends later than booked.

Return the number of the room that hosted the most meetings. On a tie, return the lowest room number.

examples.why: The meeting at 4 waits for room 2, freed at 5, and runs [5, 10). The meeting at 6 waits until 10, when rooms 1 and 2 free up together; it takes room 1. Rooms 1 and 2 both host 2 meetings, and 1 is lower.
Sorted by start: room 0, room 1, then at 3 the lowest free room is 1 again, and at 5 it is 0. Room 2 has been free the longest, but the lowest number wins, not the longest wait.
With one room every meeting ends up there, the second one delayed until 10.

hints: Sort the meetings by start time and simulate. At each meeting you need two answers fast: the lowest free room, and, if none is free, the room that frees up first.
Those are two different orders. Keep the free rooms in one min-heap by room number, and the busy rooms in another min-heap by (end time, room number).

Before placing a meeting, move every busy room whose end time is ≤ the start into the free heap. If the free heap is empty, pop the earliest busy room and push it back with end = its old end + the meeting's length.

explain.intuition:
This is a simulation, and the only question is how to answer "which room?" quickly. There are two situations, and each wants a different order. When some room is free, you want the lowest number among free rooms. When none is free, you want the earliest end time among busy rooms, breaking ties by number.

So keep two heaps: free rooms keyed by number, busy rooms keyed by (end, room). Before each meeting, release every busy room that has finished by its start. Then either take the lowest free room, or take the earliest busy room and push its end forward by the meeting's length. A delay never shortens a meeting, which is why the end is oldEnd + (end − start), not the booked end.
steps: Sort meetings by start. Put rooms 0..n−1 in the free heap; the busy heap starts empty. Keep a count per room.
For each meeting [s, e], pop busy rooms with end ≤ s and push their numbers into the free heap.
If the free heap is not empty, pop the lowest room and push (e, room) into the busy heap.
Otherwise pop the earliest (end, room) and push (end + e − s, room) back.
Increment that room's count. At the end return the room with the highest count, lowest number on ties.
pitfalls: Choosing the room that has been free the longest instead of the lowest-numbered free room. The second example breaks that.
Giving a delayed meeting its booked end time. It runs for its original length starting when the room frees up.
Treating a room as busy at the exact moment its meeting ends. The ranges are half-open, so it is free at end.

complexity.time: O(m log m + m log n)

solutions.title: Scan all rooms per meeting
solutions.idea: Keep each room's end time in an array. For every meeting, scan for the lowest free room, or else the earliest-ending one.

solutions.title: Two heaps
solutions.idea: A min-heap of free room numbers and a min-heap of busy rooms by (end, room). Release finished rooms before each meeting.
solutions.time: O(m log m + m log n)

followups: Return the minimum number of rooms needed so that no meeting is ever delayed. Which heap is enough?
Meetings may be cancelled after booking. How would you keep the heaps correct?
